articles.title: Plaintiffs Contesting Tren de Aragua Membership Claims / Alien Enemies Act Application Still Can't Sue Pseudonymously
articles.content:
From Judge James Wesley Hendrix (N.D. Tex.) Friday in W.M.M. v. Trump (for more on the earlier Fifth Circuit en banc decision, see here):
On March 14, 2025, the President invoked the Alien Enemies Act—a federal statute that permits the President to deport foreign nationals who are engaged in an "invasion or predatory incursion" against the United States—to detain and remove members of Tren de Aragua, a Venezuelan terrorist group that traffics drugs and engages in other criminal activity. The petitioners, on behalf of a proposed class of Venezuelan nationals detained under the President's Proclamation, brought a habeas action in this Court. The petitioners argue that (1) the Proclamation exceeds the President's authority under the Alien Enemies Act and (2) the detainees have not received sufficient notice to challenge their removal.
After trips to the Fifth Circuit and the U.S. Supreme Court, the matter is back before this Court…. [T]he petitioners seek leave for the proposed class representatives to proceed under pseudonyms. The Court denies that motion because the named petitioners have not substantiated their conclusory allegations with evidence that they will suffer harm if their identities are disclosed. The Fifth Circuit found the petitioners' allegations insufficient to support their request to use pseudonyms [though it] {denied the petitioners' motion "without prejudice to any future determination by the district court regarding whether to allow any new class representatives to proceed under pseudonyms"}, and the petitioners have not persuaded this Court to depart from the Fifth Circuit's sound analysis….
Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 10(a) "require[s] plaintiffs to disclose their names in the instrument they file to commence a lawsuit." "Public access to this information is more than a customary procedural formality; First Amendment guarantees are implicated when a court decides to restrict public scrutiny of judicial proceedings." … "Judicial records belong to the American people; they are public, not private, documents." … The Fifth Circuit thus recognizes a "strong presumption against party pseudonymity."
In certain circumstances, however, courts may allow parties to proceed under pseudonyms. Specifically, where a case involves "matters of a sensitive and highly personal nature," the usual practice of disclosing the parties' identities "yields 'to a policy of protecting privacy in a very private matter.'" … Additionally, the Fifth Circuit has considered whether the party has shown that he will face "possible threatened harm" if his identity is disclosed….
D.A.A., T.I.A., and E.A.A. "have not shown that disclosure of their names would require them to disclose information of the utmost intimacy." … The petitioners do not request pseudonymity because the disclosure of their identities would reveal intimate details about their religion, sexuality, or family life. Rather, the petitioners do not want to disclose their identities because they do not want to publicize their alleged connection to TdA, a terrorist organization. But the Fifth Circuit has never suggested that this kind of information counts as a "sensitive and highly personal" matter that warrants pseudonymity.
Further, the petitioners dispute their designation as members of TdA. In other words, the petitioners allege that this designation is false. Yet the Fifth Circuit has implied that pseudonymity is proper only when the sensitive information—concerning, for example, one's religious beliefs—is true. Because the petitioners' alleged connection with TdA is, in their view, not true—and because it is not the kind of information that justifies pseudonymity—this Stegall factor cuts against the petitioners.
The Fifth Circuit also rejected the petitioners' argument that courts "should treat 'immigration matters, like the ones here, that disclose personal information,' as intimate information warranting pseudonymity," because the petitioners failed to explain how revealing "immigration matters" would "'disclose [any] personal information,' let alone information that makes pseudonyms appropriate." The petitioners have not provided any additional support for this argument to justify a departure from the Fifth Circuit's conclusion.
Relatedly, the Fifth Circuit rejected the petitioners' argument that they should be allowed to proceed under pseudonyms because several petitioners are seeking asylum. Two petitioners—T.I.A. and E.A.A.—seek asylum. The petitioners cite 8 C.F.R. § 208.6(a), which provides that information contained in an application for asylum "shall not be disclosed without the written consent of the applicant." But disclosing the petitioners' names will reveal only the fact that they have applied for asylum, not any information contained in the petitioners' respective asylum applications. {The information in the petitioners' respective asylum applications would likely not come before this Court anyway because the Court "lacks jurisdiction to hear an application for asylum."} Further, the petitioners still have not "shown that Venezuela penalizes asylum seekers." …
[P]etitioners [also] argue that public disclosure of their identities would subject them to physical violence in Venezuela. The Fifth Circuit rejected this argument because the petitioners expressed "only 'generalized concerns' about potential retaliation, directed toward either them or their families, in Venezuela or other countries as a result of the U.S. government identifying them with TdA." In the Fifth Circuit's view, the petitioners failed to produce "'plausible predictions of possible future violence,' let alone evidence of 'express threats or incidents' to anyone, including them or their families, arising out of identification with TdA." The petitioners' "evidence-less, generalized fears" thus did not "overcome the presumption against pseudonymity."
The Fifth Circuit's sound conclusion follows from the principle that courts should "not usually allow parties to proceed anonymously based on generalized concerns." Indeed, the Fifth Circuit recognized that "[c]ourts generally allow pseudonymity if there is 'reasonable[]' 'fear[]' of 'retaliatory physical … harm to the requesting party or even more critically, to innocent non-parties,' which may be considered in light of 'the anonymous party's vulnerability to such retaliation.'" "Express threats of violence would likely qualify, as would specific past incidents of violence or vandalism." But the "[l]ack of such express threats or incidents—or at least lack of highly plausible predictions of possible future violence—will usually count against pseudonymity."
Seeking to surmount this hurdle, the petitioners have now provided "evidence not previously provided to the Fifth Circuit[] regarding risk of retaliation due to the government's designation" of the petitioners as members of TdA. In particular, the petitioners have provided an expert's declaration describing how TdA members face threats of physical violence from Venezuelan "paramilitary groups," "right-wing opposition leaders," and "[r]ival gangs." The expert's declaration also says that the Venezuelan government features TdA members—many of whom are detained at the Center for Terrorist Confinement (CECOT) in Tecoluca, El Salvador—in political propaganda and exposes them to political violence.
But this additional evidence still provides "only 'generalized concerns' about potential retaliation." Each petitioner asserts that he "faces serious danger" of "retaliation, coercion, extortion, threatened prosecution, and violence from [TdA]-associated groups, rival gangs, and others" in El Salvador or Venezuela. But the petitioners have identified neither "express threats or incidents" nor "highly plausible predictions of possible future violence" to support pseudonymity. And the expert's declaration suffers from the same flaw. It says that alleged members of TdA "sometimes" face physical threats from groups that oppose the Venezuelan government, and "may" face threats or attacks from rival gangs. The two-page declaration lists no "[e]xpress threats of violence" or "specific past incidents of violence or vandalism" to support its generalized assertions.
Further, while the expert's declaration suggests that the Venezuelan regime may use members of TdA detained at CECOT as "propaganda tools" and subject those detainees to "political violence," these suggestions are conclusory. The expert's declaration does not even connect (1) the potential disclosure of the petitioners' identities in this lawsuit with (2) the likelihood that the petitioners will be used as "propaganda tools" and accordingly face "political violence" in El Salvador or Venezuela. The declaration merely states that its conclusions are based on "the situation in Venezuela for the men sent by the United States to CECOT in March 2025." In this respect, the declaration suggests that the Venezuelan regime singled out these men—and "disclos[ed] personal details about them"—solely on account of their detention at CECOT. Whether the detainees' identities were disclosed in a lawsuit in the United States was of no matter.
In any event, the Court lacks sufficient evidence to support the inference that denying the petitioners' motion to proceed under pseudonyms will cause them to face threats or physical harm in the future. Thus, the petitioners have not persuaded this Court that its analysis of this issue should differ from the Fifth Circuit's, given the generalized, conclusory nature of the petitioners' allegations.
{The Court previously granted the original named petitioners' motion to proceed under pseudonyms, because of "the sensitive and personal information about their immigration status and histories in this case." But the Court did so in a summary order at the inception of this litigation on a rapid timeline. Considering the en banc Fifth Circuit's statement on this matter and the lack of compelling evidence to distinguish the petitioners' present arguments from the arguments that the Fifth Circuit found unpersuasive, the Court finds it appropriate to deny the petitioners' motion for leave to proceed under pseudonyms.}
The post Plaintiffs Contesting Tren de Aragua Membership Claims / Alien Enemies Act Application Still Can't Sue Pseudonymously appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: The Wild Turnover of the Midterms Shows That Living Life Requires Ignoring Government
articles.content:
There are lessons to take from last week's blue tidal wave which swept Republicans from power in Congress and across much of the country, just as there were from the 2024 ejection of Democrats from office. Among other things, party turnover underlines the futility of relying on government to maintain predictable conditions and to protect cherished liberties. The midterm elections may have been primarily a rejection of corruption and ineptitude among GOP officials, but they also empowered Democrats to enact an agenda in many places wildly at odds with what prevailed before.
Americans who dread the loss of school choice, violations of gun rights, and increased regulation—or who two years ago feared attacks on reproductive liberty and immigrants—must accept that much of the future of freedom requires defying and undermining intrusive government, no matter who holds office.
Last week's elections removed Republicans from office across the country, much as Democrats were crushed in 2024. Notably, Texas—recently a refuge for those fleeing Democratic dominance in California—flipped largely blue. "For the first time in more than three decades, Democrats have broken Republicans' grip on statewide elections in Texas," observed David Martin Davies of Texas Public Radio. Political refugees must wonder whether the conditions that drove them to move will follow them.
It's true that elections have consequences. But majorities have no more right to impose authoritarian visions than do solo tyrants. And it's not clear that voters booting one party from office are eager to embrace what the other major party has to offer.
Last week, the Associated Press asked voters why they cast their ballots as they did. It found "the cost of living and government corruption weighing heavily on many Americans' minds as they cast a ballot in Tuesday's midterm elections." In addition, "the survey also found that while Democrats have at least a slight advantage on several major issues, including the economy and government corruption, the Democratic Party is not much more popular among U.S. voters than the Republican Party."
Americans are hate-voting in election after election. While the shrinking ranks of hardcore partisans still like their parties, Pew Research's Steven Shepard reported last month that majorities of independents who just favor one party "say a major reason they lean toward their preferred party is that the other party's policies are harmful." But "relatively few Republican leaners (34%) and Democratic leaners (27%) say a major reason they lean toward their preferred party is the perceived good of its policies."
Even so, in our seemingly immutable two-party system, rejecting one of the political tribes means handing the reins of power to the other. Politicians aren't very good at accepting that they're regarded as slightly less awful than the alternative and acting accordingly. They always take the ball and run.
"Democrats will use their new trifecta status in Arizona, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin to dismantle union reforms, progress on taxes, school choice and litigation reform," cautions The Wall Street Journal's Kimberley Strassel.
Sure enough, Democratic governors in Arizona and Texas immediately renewed vows to roll back overwhelmingly popular school choice programs, just as their colleagues in Virginia earlier attacked that state's once robust protections for self-defense rights once they gained power.
Voters will have an opportunity in 2028 to reconsider their choices. After all, federal Republicans were spanked this year after they replaced Democrats who sent government spending and resulting inflation soaring, only to implement tariffs and a war that kept prices rising, along with unpopular immigration enforcement. But the wild political swings of recent years suggest the result will be dramatic changes in law and unstable policy environments, with more of the same to follow in the next round of elections.
That doesn't mean we should stop voting for candidates we find less bad than the alternatives; none of us want to live under intolerable governments. But to live our lives through cycles of severe policy changes, engaging in activities that are forbidden under one party and encouraged under the other, we should emulate those Americans of the past who largely ignored government dictates.
Prohibition was famously defeated by noncompliance. "There were twice as many speakeasies in Rochester, New York, as saloons closed by Prohibition. That was more or less true throughout the country," the Cato Institute's Mark Thornton noted in a 1991 analysis.
Likewise for laws against same-sex relationships. "As far back as the 1890s, there were establishments in the Village catering to lesbians and gays," Bedford + Bowery reports, although same-sex conduct wasn't fully legalized in New York until 1980. The modern gay rights movement kicked off after a fiercely resisted 1969 police raid on the Stonewall bar.
Gambling has long been targeted by law, though restrictions loosened in recent years. While many people who dislike games of chance want bans reimposed, "the result of an attempted ban, as we have seen, is that gamblers go underground," the Competitive Enterprise Institute warned in 2014.
And modern gun control laws have repeatedly met defiance, including "a compliance rate of about 4 percent" with New York's mandatory registration for so-called assault weapons as described by Hudson Valley One. The modern DIY movement to encourage people to manufacture their own firearms is specifically intended to make such laws unenforceable.
Ignoring the law isn't a completely satisfactory replacement for living under a predictable and permissive regime. There's always the risk of arrest. People have little recourse when they get ripped off or otherwise mistreated when engaged in illegal activity. And underground markets empower organized criminals, who are not the safest people to deal with.
But defying laws also helps compel political change. It forces politicians to choose between looking impotent as laws go ignored, or as if they're responsive to popular opinion. Over the years, officeholders who agreed to legalize booze, marijuana, same-sex relationships, concealed carry, and the like weren't always true believers in the cause. But they recognized unbeatable popular resistance when they saw it.
In the years to come, political power will probably continue cycling between two major parties who do their best to overreach and offend the American public. Homeschoolers, reproductive rights advocates, gun owners, and anybody else who votes in hopes of being left alone should consider the lessons of the past. The tenure of dominant parties turns rancid at a seemingly accelerating pace, but living your life as you please without regard for politicians' whims has timeless appeal.
The post The Wild Turnover of the Midterms Shows That Living Life Requires Ignoring Government appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Javier Milei: 'You Don't Beat Populism by Practicing Populism'
articles.content:
The December 2026 issue of Reason explores Argentine President Javier Milei's accomplishments and what is yet to be done.
We always say that government operates through three paths.
One of them is extremely important, and it is the one I came from: the cultural battle. All of us, in one way or another, wage that battle wherever we can, spreading the ideas of liberty and explaining the benefits of freedom.
But ideas alone aren't enough.
I remember that before getting involved in politics, I once went to dinner with someone. In the middle of dinner, this person kept saying, "Yes, very interesting, very interesting." Then he called his son and asked him to bring one of the political ballots that people use to vote. He said, "Ah, wonderful," put the ballot down in front of me, and asked, "Where are Milei's ideas on here?"
In other words, if we want to change reality, we not only have to engage in the cultural battle and spread these ideas; we also have to get involved in the political arena.
I often use the following example: You went to an Argentina match, and the stands were beautiful. The chants were beautiful. The spectacle in the stands was beautiful. But the ball didn't move.
To move the ball, we needed Lionel Messi scoring goals.
So if you understand that you need the cultural battle, then you also need political muscle. And once you reach power, you need competent administration. Because if we don't produce results, then we have a problem there too.
When you have spent a long time fighting the cultural battle, one of the greatest challenges you encounter as a policymaker is that afterward you have to take those ideas into elections and you have to produce results—knowing, moreover, that we do not use every tool in the toolbox.
And I make no apologies for that.
In fact, I am proud that we don't use every tool in the toolbox, because some of those tools are morally contemptible.
We are not going to violate the right to life. We are not going to violate liberty. We are not going to violate private property.
In fact, if you look at the recent debate, there are many people who, with the upcoming election year in mind—and they do this with good intentions, because they want to make sure we are reelected and can continue on this path—are asking us to loosen our monetary policy and fiscal policy.
And the answer is: We are not going to do that.
We are not going to loosen our fiscal policy. The fiscal result is not negotiable.
And we are not going to compromise on monetary policy either, because we are not going to stop until we have defeated inflation.
If I had to put it in a single sentence: You don't beat populism by practicing populism.
There is no substitute for good policy. There is no substitute for doing what is morally right. There is no substitute for implementing policies that are just.
What we have to do is stay on this path and let Argentines choose.
What could be better than, for the first time, Argentines having a genuine menu of options in which ideas and results can both be presented?
Because if there is one thing this government has demonstrated, it is that everything we promised, we have delivered.
We reached the midterm elections having fulfilled every campaign promise. And not only that: We ran our party for the first time in all 24 districts, won 16 of them, and beat that damned Kirchnerism by 17 points.
Therefore, good policies are not negotiable.
And it will be up to Argentines whether they want to return to the past, whether they want to embrace failure again, or whether they want to continue with this transformation that will make Argentina great again.

The December 2026 issue of Reason explores Argentine President Javier Milei's accomplishments and what is yet to be done.

We always say that government operates through three paths.

One of them is extremely important, and it is the one I came from: the cultural battle. All of us, in one way or another, wage that battle wherever we can, spreading the ideas of liberty and explaining the benefits of freedom.

But ideas alone aren't enough.

I remember that before getting involved in politics, I once went to dinner with someone. In the middle of dinner, this person kept saying, "Yes, very interesting, very interesting." Then he called his son and asked him to bring one of the political ballots that people use to vote. He said, "Ah, wonderful," put the ballot down in front of me, and asked, "Where are Milei's ideas on here?"

In other words, if we want to change reality, we not only have to engage in the cultural battle and spread these ideas; we also have to get involved in the political arena.

I often use the following example: You went to an Argentina match, and the stands were beautiful. The chants were beautiful. The spectacle in the stands was beautiful. But the ball didn't move.

To move the ball, we needed Lionel Messi scoring goals.

So if you understand that you need the cultural battle, then you also need political muscle. And once you reach power, you need competent administration. Because if we don't produce results, then we have a problem there too.

When you have spent a long time fighting the cultural battle, one of the greatest challenges you encounter as a policymaker is that afterward you have to take those ideas into elections and you have to produce results—knowing, moreover, that we do not use every tool in the toolbox.

And I make no apologies for that.

In fact, I am proud that we don't use every tool in the toolbox, because some of those tools are morally contemptible.

We are not going to violate the right to life. We are not going to violate liberty. We are not going to violate private property.

In fact, if you look at the recent debate, there are many people who, with the upcoming election year in mind—and they do this with good intentions, because they want to make sure we are reelected and can continue on this path—are asking us to loosen our monetary policy and fiscal policy.

And the answer is: We are not going to do that.

We are not going to loosen our fiscal policy. The fiscal result is not negotiable.

And we are not going to compromise on monetary policy either, because we are not going to stop until we have defeated inflation.

If I had to put it in a single sentence: You don't beat populism by practicing populism.

There is no substitute for good policy. There is no substitute for doing what is morally right. There is no substitute for implementing policies that are just.

What we have to do is stay on this path and let Argentines choose.

What could be better than, for the first time, Argentines having a genuine menu of options in which ideas and results can both be presented?

Because if there is one thing this government has demonstrated, it is that everything we promised, we have delivered.

We reached the midterm elections having fulfilled every campaign promise. And not only that: We ran our party for the first time in all 24 districts, won 16 of them, and beat that damned Kirchnerism by 17 points.

Therefore, good policies are not negotiable.

And it will be up to Argentines whether they want to return to the past, whether they want to embrace failure again, or whether they want to continue with this transformation that will make Argentina great again.

articles.title: Brickbat: Show Us Your Digital ID
articles.content:
The Office of Communications (Ofcom), the United Kingdom's communications regulator, says social media companies may have to require users to show photo ID to prove they are at least 16 years old.  The requirement would be part of the government's planned ban on social media use by those under 16, which is expected to take effect next year. Ofcom identified several ways companies could verify users' ages, such as by checking passports or drivers licenses against live images, and estimating age through facial recognition technology. However, about 150,000 16- and 17-year-olds in Britain have neither a passport nor a drivers license. Facial age estimates can also be inaccurate by several years, which Ofcom warns may require additional identification checks for youthful-looking users. Supporters argue that stronger age checks will better protect children from harmful online content, but critics raise concerns about privacy, access to social media and whether the restrictions can actually be enforced. Ofcom acknowledges that determined children will find ways around the restrictions, as has happened in Australia, where many underage users continued accessing social media despite a similar ban.
